metaDescription: Gas wood chippers from 7HP yard units to a 35HP 8 inch towable, compared on engine class, drum or disc design, start type and towing and upkeep realities.
expertTake: The SuperHandy 9HP with a 4 inch capacity and a rotating chute is the best match for most acreage owners, and the BILT HARD 15HP 420cc drum chipper is the step up when limbs reach 6 inches. The SuperHandy 7HP 3-in-1 is the budget pick for brush piles. The MechMaxx 8 inch 35HP is a contractor-class machine that most homeowners should rent, not buy.
introParagraphs: Gas power is what separates a wood chipper that clears real brush from a garden shredder. The engine sets the ceiling on limb thickness, runs anywhere on the property and keeps going when a cord would not reach.

That freedom comes with fuel, oil and a lot of vibration to manage. The sections below explain how engine size relates to capacity, what a drum design changes, and what year-three ownership looks like.

products.name: SuperHandy 9HP gas chipper, 4 inch capacity, reversible blades
products.description:
The SuperHandy 9HP is a compact rotor machine with a 4 inch limb capacity, reversible blades and a chute that adjusts through 110 degrees so you can aim chips into a bucket, tarp or bin. A 9 horsepower engine is the class where chipping 4 inch limbs becomes comfortable instead of marginal.

The tradeoff is that reversible blades mean two cutting edges, but each edge still dulls and needs regular attention. The three-in-one layout also handles leafy brush through a separate path, which is convenient but means more openings to keep clear. Compared with the 7HP SuperHandy it adds an inch of capacity and about a third more rated horsepower, which is the right margin for dry oak and maple.

As with any gas machine, plan for an oil change each season, a clean air filter and stabilizer in the fuel before storage. Blade bolts must be checked often because vibration works them loose. Because the 4 inch rating is a ceiling, feed hardwood at a slower pace and let the engine regain speed between limbs; a bogging engine tone is the cue to back off. In year three the typical issues are a worn pull cord, a fouled spark plug and dull blades, all cheap to fix if you catch them early.
products.bestFor: Properties with limbs up to 4 inches and a wish to direct the chips.
cons: More openings to keep clear of jams

products.name: EFCUT C40E 9HP 274cc electric-start chipper, 4 inch
products.description:
The C40E puts a 274cc, 9 horsepower engine behind a 4 inch throat, a 15.9 inch flywheel and an electric start button. The big flywheel stores energy, so the knives keep their speed when a dense limb enters the throat.

The tradeoff is the extra weight and the starter battery. Electric start is a clear comfort advantage on cold mornings and for owners who cannot pull a recoil cord repeatedly. Compared with the SuperHandy 9HP, the engine class is the same but the C40E adds the electric start and a heavier flywheel, which smooths out the chipping load.

Keep the starter battery on a maintainer over winter, and apply the standard routine: oil each season, air filter, spark plug and blade bolts. The heavier flywheel also means the engine keeps spinning for a few seconds after you shut it off, so wait for it to stop completely before reaching toward the chute. Expect the machine to be loud, so hearing protection is not optional.
products.bestFor: Owners who want easy starting and 4 inch capacity.

products.name: SuperHandy 7HP 3-in-1 chipper-shredder, 3 inch, slanted housing
products.description:
The SuperHandy 7HP 3-in-1 combines chipping, shredding and mulching in one frame, with a slanted housing designed to reduce jams. It offers a 15:1 reduction ratio when shredding and a 3 inch limb capacity.

The tradeoff is power. At 7 horsepower a 3 inch hardwood limb loads the engine, and feeding must be slow and steady. The slanted housing helps material flow, which matters when you shred leafy brush. Compared with the 9HP units, it is cheaper to own but has a lower ceiling.

Expect small-engine care: oil, air filter and stabilizer in the fuel. Because the housing is angled, material tends to slide through rather than hang up, but wet, stringy brush will still wrap the rotor, so cut long vines into shorter lengths first. It is a sensible first gas chipper for someone who mainly wants to clear piles of brush every spring.
products.bestFor: Brush piles and limbs to 3 inches on a budget.

products.name: BILT HARD 6 inch 15HP 420cc E-start drum chipper
products.description:
The BILT HARD drum chipper has a 420cc four-cycle OHV engine, a steel drum with a dual-blade cutting system, CR alloy steel blades and a durable anvil. It takes limbs up to 6 inches and starts with an electric button.

The tradeoff is that drum chippers are heavier and more complex than the small rotor machines. They feed more consistently and chip faster, but they need more power and more upkeep. A 420cc single is about the 14 to 15 horsepower class, which is the usual minimum for 6 inch chippers. Compared with the 9HP 4 inch units, it adds two inches of capacity and a lot more mass.

Check blade clearance to the anvil, grease any bearings and keep the starter battery charged. Because drum machines are heavier, plan a safe way to move them: ramps, a tractor or a strong helper, never a steep slope with the machine unchained. Sharpen on a schedule, because a dull drum knife overloads the belt or clutch long before the engine complains.
products.bestFor: Heavy cleanup with limbs up to 6 inches.

products.name: MechMaxx 8 inch 35HP 1000cc E-start towable chipper
products.description:
The MechMaxx B200 has a 1000cc, 35 horsepower air-cooled OHV engine, an 8 inch capacity, electric start, a trailer bar and 19 inch front and 13 inch rear wheels. This is the size at which a machine begins to look like a small tree-service unit.

The tradeoff is that it needs space, towing capacity and the discipline of a heavy machine. 8 inch limbs will test the whole drivetrain, and the operator needs proper protective equipment and a clear drop zone. Compared with the 15HP 6 inch machine, it handles two more inches but costs far more to own and move.

Check tire pressure, hitch and lighting before any tow. Keep the starter battery charged and follow the oil schedule. A machine of this size also needs a clear feed area, ear and eye protection, a hard hat and chaps or sturdy clothing without loose cuffs, and it is worth reading the manual twice before the first start. For most homeowners the sensible alternative is to rent this class for a weekend.
products.bestFor: Large properties or small contractors with 6 to 8 inch limbs.

products.name: GARDENBEAUT S3 7HP 212cc chipper, 3 inch, 15:1
products.description:
The GARDENBEAUT S3 is a 7 horsepower, 212cc gas chipper-shredder with a 15:1 reduction ratio, a vertical extended hopper and a 3 inch limb capacity. It is built to be lighter than steel-heavy rivals, which makes it easier to roll across a lawn and tuck into a shed.

The tradeoff is the same as the other 7HP machines: it is happiest on green limbs and brush up to about 2 inches, and it will bog on dry 3 inch hardwood unless you feed slowly. A horizontal-shaft 212cc engine is a common, well-supported design, so spark plugs, air filters and carburetor parts are easy to find. Compared with the SuperHandy 7HP 3-in-1, the layout is similar but the vertical hopper is the main difference, since it keeps the footprint small.

Store it with the fuel valve off and stabilizer in the tank, keep the engine oil fresh and check the blade bolts after the first few hours of running.
products.bestFor: Light acreage with limbs up to about 3 inches and limited storage room.

buyingCriteria.explanation: As a rule, 7HP engines pair with 3 inch machines, 9HP with 4 inch, 14 to 15HP with 6 inch and 35HP with 8 inch. The SuperHandy 7HP, SuperHandy 9HP, BILT HARD 420cc and MechMaxx 1000cc fit this ladder. Buying one class above your thickest limb avoids pinning the engine. A common mistake is buying for the one big limb you cut every ten years; size for the 80 to 90 percent of work you actually do.

Small-engine horsepower claims are often gross figures. Displacement is a better check: 212cc is about 7HP, 274cc about 9HP, 420cc about 15HP and 1000cc about 35HP. If a listing claims much more horsepower than its displacement implies, treat the claim with suspicion. Net power ratings, where listed, are more honest than gross ones, and a machine that publishes net kilowatts is easier to compare.

Small rotor machines, like the SuperHandy units, are simple and compact. Drum chippers like the BILT HARD feed material more evenly and process more per minute, but need more engine. For 3 to 4 inch work a rotor is fine; for 6 inches a drum is better. Drums also shred leafy brush more consistently because the material is fed by the drum, not left to gravity.

Recoil starts are simple and have no battery, but big engines are hard to pull. Electric start, on the EFCUT, BILT HARD and MechMaxx, is worth having from 9HP up. Keep the battery on a maintainer. A weak starter battery is the single most common reason an electric-start chipper will not start in spring.

A trailer bar and big wheels, as on the MechMaxx, help move a heavy machine across a property. Even then, a 1000cc machine is difficult to push by hand on soft ground, so plan where it will work before you pull it there. Many small units are not rated for highway towing, so check lighting, tires and local rules.

Blades must be reached for sharpening, and hoppers must have guards. Reversible blades, as on the SuperHandy 9HP, give two edges. Check for an emergency stop on larger machines. Never defeat a guard, and keep a long push stick within reach so that your hands never go near the throat.

howWeEvaluated.title: Engine and capacity
howWeEvaluated.description: We matched engine displacement to rated capacity, from 212cc at 3 inches to 1000cc at 8 inches. Units with high capacity claims on small engines were noted. We also gave extra weight to anything that gave a net power figure.

howWeEvaluated.title: Cutting system
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared rotor and drum designs, flywheel size and blade types. Reversible blades and a heavy flywheel scored higher.

howWeEvaluated.title: Start and handling
howWeEvaluated.description: We weighed electric start, wheels and tow bars against weight.

howWeEvaluated.title: Safety
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at emergency stops, hopper design and chute control. Larger machines were expected to have a quick-stop control near the feed point, and the MechMaxx lists one.

howWeEvaluated.title: Ownership
howWeEvaluated.description: Based on the spec sheet and owner feedback patterns, we weighed fuel care, blade upkeep and parts supply.

cards.label: Rotor
cards.text: The SuperHandy and EFCUT rotor machines are compact and simple. They suit limbs to 4 inches.

cards.label: Drum
cards.text: The BILT HARD drum feeds evenly and chips faster, but needs more engine. It suits 6 inch limbs.

howToChoose.note: Rotor for yard work. Drum for heavy cleanup.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: Look for 4 inch capacity or more, a flywheel to carry hard limbs and a way to move the machine to the pile.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The EFCUT C40E and BILT HARD 6 inch fit best. The MechMaxx suits very large storm jobs.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: Spend more if you regularly cut limbs over 4 inches. The BILT HARD 6 inch and MechMaxx are the step up.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: Save if limbs are 3 inches or less. The SuperHandy 7HP is enough.

maintenance.why: Chipping loads run small engines hot.

faq.q: What engine size do I need?
faq.a: Roughly 7HP for 3 inch, 9HP for 4 inch, 15HP for 6 inch and 35HP for 8 inch. Pick one size above your thickest limb.

faq.q: Is a drum better than a rotor?
faq.a: Drums feed more evenly and chip faster but need more power. Rotors are simpler and cheaper for smaller limbs.
From about 9HP, it is a real convenience. Below that recoil is fine.

faq.q: Can I tow it on the road?
faq.a: Many small units have no road rating. Check lighting, tires and local rules first.
Every 10 to 15 hours of running, sooner on dirty or dry hardwood.
If you chip a pile once a year, renting a larger machine can cost less than owning.
